tldr: This study achieves stable, sustained grasping with a shape memory polymer (SMP)-based variable-stiffness soft gripper by combining a physical model with machine learning to compensate for grasping force decay caused by material stress relaxation.
hero_caption: Overall view of the soft gripper inspired by octopus compliance and suction capabilities. It illustrates the mechanism--AI co-design pipeline integrating a structure supporting multi-mode grasping, multimodal perception using a camera and thermal imaging, and physics-informed learning-based force control.
overview:
Soft robotic hands offer huge advantages in compliantly adapting to unknown or fragile objects for safe grasping. However, the polymers responsible for this flexibility exhibit viscoelasticity, leading to stress relaxation—a continuous decay of internal force during sustained holding at a fixed posture. Furthermore, incorporating shape memory polymers (SMPs) that vary stiffness with heat dramatically changes not only deformation but also relaxation dynamics depending on temperature, making stable, long-duration force maintenance extremely difficult.

To solve this, the authors drew inspiration from human grasping, which switches muscle stiffness while using sensory feedback to compensate for force decay. First, they placed an RGB camera and an infrared thermal camera at the base of the fingers, creating a non-contact multimodal perception system that does not compromise soft structure compliance. Next, they introduced a reduced viscoelastic model separating contact force into an instantaneous elastic force and a time-dependent relaxation component, and developed a two-stage machine learning pipeline (ICFN and RCFN) to predict their parameters in real time from camera images and the temperature field.

In real-robot experiments with a 280-second grasp-and-hold task, the proposed method kept the force tracking error down to a mean absolute error (MAE) of 0.066 N—just 1.32% of the 5 N target. This represents an 80% error reduction over an uncompensated fixed-aperture baseline and 95% over an instantaneous-only baseline. The work clearly demonstrates the effectiveness of coupling structural compliance with AI-driven dynamic compensation in soft robotics.
contributions: Developed a bio-inspired soft finger integrating passive compliance, thermal variable stiffness (SMP), and switchable adhesive pads into a single structure capable of transitioning among three modes: high stiffness, compliant, and suction-assisted.

Built a multimodal perception system by mounting an RGB camera and an infrared thermography sensor at the finger base, capturing deformation and the temperature field non-invasively and synchronously without impeding soft structure deformation.

Proposed a physics-informed learning framework using a reduced viscoelastic force representation derived from a temperature-coupled generalized Maxwell--Wiechert model, decoupling instantaneous contact force prediction (ICFN) from relaxation parameter estimation (RCFN) to compensate for long-duration force decay.

Achieved an MAE of 0.066 N in a 280-second sustained grasping test, demonstrating high-precision force control tailored to stiffness states across a wide range—from feather-light touch (0.3 N) to heavy-payload grasping (5--6 N).

sections.heading: Grasping Compliantly, Holding Firmly: A Finger Mechanism Uniting Variable Stiffness and Non-Contact Sensing
sections.summary: The paper introduces a soft finger combining a passive compliant skeleton, shape memory polymer (SMP), and adhesive pads. Instead of embedding sensors inside the finger, observing deformation and temperature from the base via cameras preserves compliance while enabling simultaneous measurement.
sections.details:
The biggest headaches in soft gripper design are the trade-off between softness and load support, and the loss of compliance when embedding sensors. This paper overcomes these challenges through structural innovation in a gripper made of two identical fingers.

The finger skeleton adopts an open-frame mesh architecture with axially aligned beams and flexible joints. This provides omnidirectional passive shape adaptation, conforming compliantly to objects without precision positioning. Because the interior is hollow, it also acts as a sensing corridor that keeps the camera's field of view clear.

Stiffness switching is handled by thermally responsive SMP beams embedded inside the skeleton. Modulating their temperature with an integrated heater allows continuous transitions between a highly compliant mode and a load-bearing high-stiffness mode without altering geometric structure or applying external forces. In addition, thermally activated adhesive pads on the finger surface enable suction-assisted grasping for flat objects.

The perception system is entirely concentrated at the finger base mount. An RGB camera tracks ArUco markers placed inside the finger to monitor overall deformation (proprioception), while an infrared thermography sensor non-invasively measures the SMP beam temperature field in real time. Because no sensor elements or wires are embedded in the soft body itself, repeated large deformations carry no risk of wire breakage or unwanted stiffness changes.

captions.F2: Exploded view and grasping configurations of a single finger. It shows the open-frame compliant skeleton, embedded SMP beams, base-mounted RGB and infrared cameras, and interior ArUco markers.
captions.F3: Three grasping modes (compliant, rigid, suction-assisted) enabled by stiffness modulation and adhesion, along with their usage. In high-stiffness mode, the fingertips can hold a 1 kg weight and withstand manual perturbations, while in compliant mode, easily deformable empty cans can be grasped without crushing.

sections.heading: Why Does the Force Drop? Combating Stress Relaxation in Real Time with Physics and Learning
sections.summary: The authors derived a mathematical model that decouples contact force into an instantaneous elastic response and a time-dependent viscoelastic relaxation term. They built a two-stage lightweight neural network pipeline to estimate these parameters, enabling anticipatory force estimation and PID control at an ultra-low latency of ~5 ms.
sections.details:
The continuous decay of grasping force when holding an object at a fixed displacement stems from material stress relaxation caused by viscoelasticity. This section explains how mathematical modeling and machine learning work together to tackle this issue.

- Viscoelastic Modeling under Displacement Control (III-A):
The authors began with a generalized Maxwell--Wiechert model consisting of an equilibrium spring and $N$ Maxwell elements (spring and damper in series) placed in parallel, all with temperature dependence. Viewing the post-contact holding phase as a step displacement input $X_0$, the force in each element decays exponentially over time, and total force becomes the sum of the equilibrium elastic force and the relaxation forces of each branch.

- Reduced Temperature-Coupled Relaxation Representation (III-B):
Identifying numerous relaxation time constants on a real robot is impractical. Therefore, the authors derived a reduced model that neglects fast modes that decay quickly and approximates behavior with a single effective mode dominant over practical timescales. Defining the instantaneous contact force at the onset of holding as $F_{\mathrm{inst}}$, the force at time $t$ is expressed as $F(t) = F_{\mathrm{inst}} - K(T)(1 - e^{-t/\tau(T)})$. Here, $K(T)$ is the effective relaxation amplitude and $\tau(T)$ is the effective relaxation time constant, both strongly dependent on temperature $T$. Decoupling the instantaneous elastic force from the subsequent relaxation loss is the core of this approach.

- Physics-Informed Learning and Force Control Pipeline (III-C):
Based on this reduced model, two complementary networks were designed. The first, the Instantaneous Contact Force Network (ICFN), predicts $F_{\mathrm{inst}}$ from initial contact marker poses, deformation, beam temperature, and spatial gradients. The second, the Relaxation Compensation Force Network (RCFN), takes initial and current marker poses, velocities, and temperatures as inputs, using lightweight Ridge regression to predict $K$ and $\log \tau$. The estimated effective force $F_{\mathrm{eff}} = F_{\mathrm{inst}} - F_{\mathrm{relax}}$ is fed into a PID controller to maintain the target grasping force via motor velocity commands. Inference takes roughly 1.3 ms for ICFN and 0.14 ms for RCFN, achieving an ultra-fast total real-time loop time of around 4.94 ms.

captions.F4: Overall pipeline for physics-informed learning and force control. (a) Structure of ICFN for instantaneous force and RCFN for relaxation parameters, (b) data flow merging 30 Hz RGB video and 1 Hz thermal imaging with ~5 ms inference timing, and (c) closed-loop system integrating PID force control with temperature control.

sections.heading: Putting It to the Test: From Stiffness Benchmarks to 280-Second Holds and Multi-Stage Tasks
sections.summary: Experiments included measuring finger material properties with a robot arm, evaluating force and relaxation estimation on an unseen dataset, a 280-second extended holding test, and multi-stage manipulation tasks with objects of varying stiffness. The proposed approach reduced errors by 80% to 95% compared to baselines.
sections.details:
This section evaluates the framework across diverse experimental setups.

- Temperature-Dependent Stiffness Characterization (IV-A):
A UR5e robot measured the finger's deformation profile across 27--60 °C and 2--8 N. Raising the temperature from 27 °C to 60 °C caused local stiffness to drop by 35--45% and total deformation to increase by 73%, quantitatively confirming large thermal stiffness shifts.

- Accuracy of Force Perception and Relaxation Reconstruction (IV-B):
On unseen test data, ICFN achieved an MAE of 0.651 N across 0--10 N (a full-scale error of 6.51%) with a coefficient of determination $R^2=0.848$. For relaxation trajectory reconstruction, RCFN achieved a median normalized root-mean-square error (NRMSE) of 0.118, a median relative cumulative drift (AUC_rel) of 0.049, and an average correlation coefficient of 0.990. Repeated trials at 40 °C, 50 °C, and 60 °C demonstrated strong repeatability.

- Sustained Force Tracking and Relaxation-Aware Control (IV-C):
A challenging 280-second hold was performed on a spherical unit equipped with internal pressure sensors. Without active control (fixed aperture), force steadily decayed due to stress relaxation. Instantaneous-only estimation (ICFN alone) significantly overestimated true force as relaxation progressed. In contrast, the proposed method (ICFN + RCFN) maintained highly accurate grasping in the steady-state regime (100--280 s) with an MAE of 0.066 N (only 1.32% of the 5 N target). This cuts tracking error by 80.2% over the uncompensated baseline (MAE 0.333 N) and 95.0% over the uncompensated instantaneous baseline (MAE 1.327 N).

- Real-Time Force Perception and Complex Manipulation (IV-D, IV-E):
The system demonstrated appropriate force regulation matched to finger stiffness, spanning feather-light contact (~0.3 N) up to lifting oranges and a heavy hammer (5 N). Furthermore, a multi-stage task showed thermal imaging distinguishing cold and hot water cups without contact, followed by grasping a paper cup in compliant mode to pour water, and switching to high-stiffness mode to hand over a heavy glass mug to a person.

captions.F6: Accuracy evaluation of force perception and relaxation modeling. (a, b) Parity plot and load-binned error for ICFN instantaneous force estimation, (c, d) RCFN NRMSE and AUC_rel distributions, (e, f) fits and repeatability of relaxation trajectory reconstruction across various initial loads and temperatures.
captions.F7: 280-second sustained force tracking benchmark. Force profiles for (b) fixed aperture, (c) instantaneous estimation without relaxation compensation, and (d) the proposed method. Only the proposed method closely tracks the 5 N target (blue solid line) with near-zero steady-state error, as clearly shown in distributions (e, f).

Demonstrations show coordinated stiffness and force control ranging from delicate contact detection (feathers, brushes) to high-stiffness hammer grasping (5 N), medium-stiffness orange holding, and zero-deformation balloon grasping in compliant mode (0.3 N).

sections.heading: Wrapping Up: Mechanism--AI Co-Design Shaping the Future of Soft Robotics
sections.summary: This work establishes an integrated framework of structure, perception, and learning to overcome long-duration force decay in thermally coupled viscoelastic soft hands. Future extensions include broader hand morphologies and deeper exploration of material-level physics.
sections.details:
This paper presents a comprehensive solution combining hardware design and physics-informed machine learning to address stress relaxation and sustained force decay—a long-standing hurdle in soft robotic grasping.

On the hardware side, passive compliance from an open skeleton, stiffness tuning via SMP, adhesion from switchable pads, and non-invasive multimodal sensing via base-mounted cameras are unified into a single system. On the software side, introducing a reduced formula based on the Maxwell--Wiechert model constrains the learning model with physical priors, allowing anticipatory relaxation compensation with only a few milliseconds of latency.

The philosophy of Mechanism--AI Co-design—where mechanisms shape the domain of feasible interactions and learning compensates for uncertain material dynamics—offers a powerful roadmap for future soft robotics. Moving forward, the authors plan to extend this method to diverse morphologies such as complex multi-fingered hands, and to further investigate the microscopic physical mechanisms coupling heat and viscoelasticity.

takeaways: Stress relaxation (force decay) is inevitable when using soft polymers; since fixed-displacement holding fails over time, feedback loops that explicitly compensate for time-dependent relaxation are essential.

Rather than forcing sensors into flexible structures, mounting cameras at the base to inspect internal deformation and thermal fields non-invasively provides an exceptionally robust and practical sensing architecture for soft robots.

Instead of delegating all viscoelastic dynamics to a black-box neural network, grounding the pipeline in a reduced Maxwell--Wiechert model allows lightweight models (like Ridge regression) to combine high generalization with millisecond inference speeds.
limitations: Stiffness modulation via SMP heating and cooling is bounded by physical thermal conduction limits, preventing instantaneous stiffness transitions and requiring timescales on the order of seconds to tens of seconds.

The experimental validation focused primarily on rigid spheres and simply shaped objects, leaving interactions where the grasped object itself possesses viscoelasticity or large plastic deformation unexamined.
Because the optical setup relies on a clear line of sight to internal markers from the base, severe torsional twisting or occlusions like dust could potentially lead to marker loss.
